title: I’m Still Convinced the iPod Was the Perfect Gadget
gist: On the iPod's 25th anniversary, Steven Levy argues it was the perfect gadget because it did one thing superbly and never distracted users, unlike the smartphone that replaced it. Tony Fadell says Apple killed it by prioritizing higher-value products, yet agrees the gap is unfilled and that the iPod made the iPhone, and so modern Apple, possible.

insights.claim: The iPod's end was set in motion when Jobs announced the iPhone on January 11, 2007, with an iPod built in, making the standalone device live on borrowed time.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Illustrates how a flagship product can cannibalize its predecessor line.
insights.locator: All these final dates were an inevitable consequence

insights.claim: Apple discontinued the classic iPod in 2014, the Nano and Shuffle in 2017, and the iPod Touch in 2022, so the exact date of death is ambiguous.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Shows a gradual product wind-down rather than a single event.
insights.locator: The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable

insights.claim: Fadell says iPod sales mattered less to Apple's bottom line once the iPhone, Mac boost and iPad appeared, and Jobs and Tim Cook, as relentless prioritizers, saw little reason to keep it.
insights.speaker: Tony Fadell
insights.so_what: Apple culls lower-value lines even when they are beloved, a pattern for portfolio decisions.
insights.quote: The discussion was about Apple [not] doing lower-value things
insights.locator: With the iPhone proving to be a monster success

insights.claim: The iPod was a one-function device that executed that function superbly and brought unconditional happiness, while smartphones gobble attention, contribute to doomscrolling and depression, and distract drivers.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Single-purpose devices hold appeal as a counterpoint to attention-maximizing phones.
insights.locator: Still, for years, Apple sold millions more

insights.claim: Fadell argues the iPod's value came from not being internet-connected, so it never distracted the listener, unlike today's connected devices.
insights.speaker: Tony Fadell
insights.so_what: Points to latent demand for disconnected, focused devices.
insights.quote: Because the iPod wasn't connected, you didn’t have all these other things going on to distract you.
insights.locator: In retrospect, he says, what made the iPod invaluable

insights.claim: Jobs redesigned the iPod almost every year, with mini, nano and shuffle in new shapes and colors, a total reshaping that iPhone updates have lacked.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Shows product reinvention cadence drove excitement that incremental iPhone updates do not.
insights.locator: Adding to the excitement was Steve Jobs’

insights.claim: Fadell says the iPhone and thus the modern Apple would never have existed without the iPod, which turned a limited computer company into a consumer electronics giant.
insights.speaker: Tony Fadell
insights.so_what: Frames a hit product as the foundation of Apple's present scale.
insights.quote: The iPhone never would have existed without it
insights.locator: I ask Fadell how he regards the iPod’s legacy

insights.claim: Communities on Facebook and Reddit mod old iPods with flash drives and Bluetooth, and an app makes iPhones mimic the iPod Classic, evidence of lingering demand.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Enthusiast modding signals an unserved niche for dedicated music players.
insights.locator: A lot of people seem to agree

insights.claim: Levy says new Apple CEO John Ternus has no incentive to revive the iPod.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Don't expect Apple to relaunch a dedicated music player.
insights.locator: I suspect a lot of others might like
